conflicts.learnSays: Job-level `concurrency` only applies within a workflow run, not across runs.
conflicts.docsSay: `jobs.<job_id>.concurrency` ensures that only a single job or workflow using the same concurrency group runs at a time, across runs.

conflicts.learnSays: Production deployments are serialized with `concurrency: group: production` and `cancel-in-progress: true`.
conflicts.docsSay: `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels the run that is already in progress when a new one starts. Without it, the new run waits as pending.

conflicts.learnSays: A `preToolUse` hook is one JSON object with `hook`, `tools` and `rules`; a guardrail workflow tests for `github-copilot[bot]`; `copilot agent run CodeAgent --allow-tool 'read,search'` gates tools.
conflicts.docsSay: Hook files use `version: 1` with a `hooks` object and commands that return a `permissionDecision`. The examples in the module are illustrative; check the hooks reference and the Copilot CLI reference for real syntax.

conflicts.learnSays: A workflow invokes the agent with `npx @github/copilot-cli`, `permissions: contents: read` and `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`.
conflicts.docsSay: The package is `@github/copilot` and the command is `copilot`. With the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`, the workflow also needs `copilot-requests: write`, and the organization policy must allow it. The alternative is a personal access token with the Copilot Requests permission in `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`.

conflicts.learnSays: A parent agent lists its subagents in `agents` and invokes them with `handoffs` in the frontmatter of its profile.
conflicts.docsSay: `handoffs` is a property of custom agents in VS Code and other IDEs. Copilot cloud agent ignores it, and the reference for GitHub does not list `agents`. On GitHub, the `agent` tool alias is what allows a custom agent to invoke another one.

conflicts.learnSays: Copilot in the cloud only has access to the repository where it is working.
conflicts.docsSay: That holds for sessions that run on GitHub Actions. Sessions that run in a cloud sandbox can work across multiple repositories.

questions.stem:
A custom agent named `planner` has the following agent profile in a GitHub repository named Repo1.

```yaml
---
name: planner
description: Produces an implementation plan and delegates the work
tools: ["read", "search"]
---
```

The planner must be able to hand the implementation to another custom agent named `implementer`. The planner must remain unable to change files or to run commands.

You need to identify the tool that the planner requires. Which configuration should you use?

options.text: `tools: ["read", "search", "execute"]`
options.rationale: Incorrect. `execute` runs shell commands, which the planner must not be able to do.

options.text: `tools: ["read", "search", "agent"]`
options.rationale: Correct. The `agent` alias allows a different custom agent to be invoked to accomplish a task, and it adds no ability to edit files or to run commands.

options.text: `tools: ["read", "search", "implementer"]`
options.rationale: Incorrect. `implementer` is not a tool name. Unrecognized tool names are ignored, so nothing changes.

options.text: `tools: ["read", "search", "edit"]`
options.rationale: Incorrect. `edit` lets the planner change files, and it does not let the planner invoke another agent.

questions.explanation: The `tools` property is the capability boundary of an agent, and delegation is a capability of its own. To hand work to another custom agent, the planner needs the `agent` tool alias. The planner stays read-only for files, because `edit` and `execute` are still absent from the list.
questions.takeaway: Delegation needs the `agent` tool. Keep `edit` and `execute` away from planning agents.

evidence.quote: Delegation boundary: which subagents can be invoked and how handoffs occur
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.quote: Use read-only toolsets for planning and review agents.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.note: The reference lists the tool aliases for custom agents. `agent` allows a different custom agent to be invoked to accomplish a task, `execute` runs a command in the shell, and `edit` allows file edits. All unrecognized tool names are ignored.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Identify required tools

clues.text: The bullet asks to identify the tools that an agent requires.
Docs list the tool aliases: `agent` invokes another custom agent, `execute` runs commands, `edit` changes files.
The name of the other agent looks like a tool name. Unrecognized names are ignored.

questions.stem:
You are writing a task contract for an agent that remediates a vulnerable dependency in a GitHub repository named Repo1.

Which part of the task contract should contain each item?

targets.text: The link to the security alert that describes the vulnerability
targets.rationale: The alert is context that the agent needs before it starts, so it is an input.

targets.text: A pull request that contains a structured plan, a bounded set of commits, and links to the workflow run
targets.rationale: The plan, the pull request and the evidence are what the agent produces.

targets.text: The vulnerable version is no longer in use, and the required checks pass
targets.rationale: This states how the result is evaluated, and it reflects the real intent of the task.

targets.text: The rule that workflow files must stay unchanged unless the platform team reviews the change
targets.rationale: A constraint is given to the agent with the task. It is an input, even though it reads like a condition for acceptance.

questions.explanation: A task contract has three parts. Inputs are what the agent needs: the context of the issue, the constraints and the boundaries. Outputs are what the agent produces: the plan, the pull request and the evidence. Success criteria say how the result is evaluated. Constraints belong to the inputs, which is the item that is easiest to misplace.
questions.takeaway: Inputs = context, constraints, boundaries. Outputs = plan, pull request, evidence. Success criteria = how the result is evaluated.

evidence.quote: Inputs: what the agent needs (issue context, constraints, boundaries).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 3

evidence.quote: Outputs: what the agent produces (plan + PR + evidence).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 3

evidence.quote: Success criteria: how results are evaluated (checks, scans, review outcomes).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 3

evidence.quote: Constraints: no workflow changes without platform review; no secrets introduced; no direct-to-main pushes.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 3

whyExam.skill: Define inputs, outputs, and success criteria for agents

clues.text: The bullet and the title of M2 unit 3 are almost identical.
The unit gives a complete example task contract, with each item under its heading.
Constraints read like acceptance conditions, but the unit lists them under Inputs.

questions.stem:
A GitHub repository named Repo1 has a workflow named `CI Validation` that builds and tests the pull requests of a dependency agent. You are creating a second workflow that runs a security agent.

You need to ensure that the second workflow starts when `CI Validation` finishes, and that the `validate` job runs only if `CI Validation` succeeded.

How should you complete the workflow?
questions.template:
name: Security Validation

on:
  workflow_run:
    [[key]]: [CI Validation]
    types:
      - [[type]]

jobs:
  validate:
    if: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.[[prop]] == 'success' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./executors/security_agent.sh

key.rationale: `workflows` names the workflow whose runs start this one. `needs` orders jobs inside one workflow, and `branches` only filters by branch.

type.rationale: `completed` starts the workflow when the other run has finished. `requested` and `in_progress` fire before a result exists.

prop.rationale: The result of the triggering run is in `github.event.workflow_run.conclusion`. Without the condition, the job would also run after a failed `CI Validation`.

questions.explanation: Sequential orchestration is used when the output of one step must be validated before the next step proceeds. `workflow_run` with `types: [completed]` starts the second workflow when the first one finishes, whatever its result. To continue only after success, the job needs a condition on the conclusion of the triggering run.
questions.takeaway: `workflow_run` fires on every completion. Gate on `github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success'`.

evidence.quote: Use this pattern when one agent's output must be validated before another step can proceed.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 3

evidence.quote: A workflow run is triggered regardless of the conclusion of the previous workflow.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

evidence.quote: If you want to run a job or step based on the result of the triggering workflow, you can use a conditional with the `github.event.workflow_run.conclusion` property.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Apply an orchestration pattern to coordinate multiple agents

clues.text: M4 unit 3 shows `workflow_run` with `workflows` and `types: [completed]`.
Docs: the workflow runs regardless of the conclusion of the previous one.

questions.stem:
A ruleset for the `main` branch of a GitHub repository named Repo1 requires a status check named `build`. The check is reported by the following workflow.

```yaml
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - 'src/**'
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: dotnet test
```

Agents and developers open pull requests in Repo1. A developer who has write access to Repo1 opens a pull request from a branch of Repo1 that changes only `README.md`. No run of `ci` starts. The merge box shows the following status for `build`.

```text
Expected — Waiting for status to be reported
```

You need to identify why the pull request is blocked. What is the cause?

options.text: The workflow was skipped by its path filter, so the required check stays pending.
options.rationale: Correct. The pull request changes no file under `src/`, so the workflow does not run and `build` is never reported. A required check that is not reported blocks merging.

options.text: The `build` job was skipped by a condition, and a skipped job blocks merging.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The job has no condition. Also, a job that is skipped by a condition reports Success and does not block merging.

options.text: The workflow waits for a maintainer to select **Approve and run workflows**.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That approval applies to the pull requests of the cloud agent and of some outside contributors, not to a collaborator's branch in the same repository. Here the workflow was filtered out by `paths`.

options.text: A required status check must be reported by a workflow that runs on `push`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Checks from workflows that run on `pull_request` are evaluated for required status checks.

questions.explanation: The evidence is in the Checks area of the pull request: the check is missing, not failing. A workflow that is skipped by a path filter, a branch filter or a commit message leaves its checks pending, and the pull request stays blocked. The fix is to avoid requiring a workflow that can be skipped, for example by removing the filter and deciding inside the job what to run.
questions.takeaway: Workflow skipped by a filter → required check stays pending and blocks. Job skipped by `if` → reports Success.

evidence.quote: Check the "Checks" tab for failed workflows
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Whether workflow checks are failing or missing
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 3

evidence.quote: A pull request that only changes a file in the repository root will not trigger this workflow. If `build` is required, the pull request is blocked with "Waiting for status to be reported."
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Identify failures by using logs, plans, traces, outputs, and workflow artifacts

clues.text: The troubleshooting page for required status checks has this exact example.
A skipped job reports Success. A skipped workflow leaves the check pending. The two are easy to swap.
A candidate who passed the live exam (Aug 2026) reported this topic: reading logs and status to diagnose a problem.

items.solution: You add the following sentence to the custom instructions of Repo1: "Never run terraform destroy." You do not use `policy.json`.
items.explanation: An instruction is guidance for the model. Nothing blocks the command when the agent does not follow it.

items.solution: You commit `policy.json` to the `.github/hooks/` folder on the default branch of Repo1.
items.explanation: The cloud agent loads hook configuration from `.github/hooks/*.json` in the repository. The `preToolUse` hook runs before each tool call, and a decision of `deny` blocks the call.

items.solution: You save `policy.json` in the `~/.copilot/hooks/` folder on your computer.
items.explanation: That is the user-level folder of Copilot CLI on one machine. The cloud agent runs in its own sandbox, which contains only the hook files of the cloned repository.

questions.explanation: A policy is enforced only by a control that runs independently of the model. A `preToolUse` hook is that control: it inspects each tool call before execution and can deny it. Where the hook file is stored decides which surface it governs. For the cloud agent, the only hook configuration that exists is the one in `.github/hooks/` of the repository, and the file must be on the default branch.
questions.takeaway: Blocking needs a `preToolUse` hook that denies. For the cloud agent, the hook file lives in `.github/hooks/` on the default branch.

evidence.quote: Decision guidance: Use enforceable hooks for blocking. Logging and banners are helpful, but they don't prevent execution.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 3

evidence.quote: Hooks provide enforceable control points that operate independently of the model's reasoning. Instead of relying on instructions, they ensure that certain rules are always applied during execution.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.quote: Hook configuration is loaded from `.github/hooks/*.json` files in the cloned repository.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

evidence.quote: The sandbox does not ship with user-level hook files, `settings.json`, `config.json`, or installed plugins.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

evidence.note: The hooks configuration file must be present on the default branch of the repository to be used by Copilot cloud agent.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Block actions that violate defined security, compliance, or Responsible AI policies

clues.text: The bullet names blocking.
M6 unit 3 decision guidance: use enforceable hooks for blocking.

Docs state where each surface loads hook files from.

questions.scenario:
You have a GitHub repository named Repo1. A ruleset for `main` requires a pull request and a status check named `build`. In the ruleset, **Require branches to be up to date before merging** is not selected. An agent opened a pull request last week, and `build` passed at that time. Since then, several other pull requests have been merged into `main`.

You need to ensure that the agent's pull request can be merged only if `build` passed with the latest changes of `main`.

items.solution: In the ruleset, you select **Require branches to be up to date before merging**.
items.explanation: The required check becomes strict. The pull request branch must be brought up to date with `main`, which adds a commit, and `build` must pass on that commit before merging.

items.solution: You re-run all jobs of the workflow run that reported `build` for the pull request.
items.explanation: A re-run uses the same commit SHA and the same Git ref as the original run. It validates the code of last week again, not the code that includes the latest changes of `main`.

items.solution: You add a `concurrency` group with `cancel-in-progress: true` to the workflow that reports `build`.
items.explanation: A concurrency group controls runs that overlap in time. It does not require the branch to contain the latest changes of `main`.

questions.explanation: A pull request that is behind its base branch carries stale context: its check results describe code that no longer exists on `main`. A strict required status check prevents this, because the branch must be up to date before merging and the check must pass on the updated branch. Running the old run again repeats the old validation.
questions.takeaway: Stale check results: require branches to be up to date before merging. A re-run uses the same commit as before.

evidence.quote: A pull request is outdated compared to the base branch
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

evidence.quote: GitHub enforces some of this automatically through features like required status checks and branch protection rules, which may require branches to be up to date before merging.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

evidence.quote: The topic branch must be up to date with the base branch before merging.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

evidence.quote: The workflow will also use the same `GITHUB_SHA` (commit SHA) and `GITHUB_REF` (git ref) of the original event that triggered the workflow run.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Prevent stale context

clues.text: "Prevent stale context" is a named bullet.
M5 unit 4 lists an outdated pull request as stale context and mentions the up-to-date requirement.
Docs define strict status checks, and state that a re-run uses the same commit SHA.

questions.stem:
Your company plans to let developers use only approved MCP servers in their IDEs. The developers must discover the servers from a custom MCP registry.

Which four actions should be performed in sequence?

items.text: The company creates or hosts an MCP registry that lists the approved servers.
An owner enters the registry URL in the Copilot policy settings and selects **Registry only**.
A developer opens an MCP-capable IDE, and the client discovers the approved servers from the registry.
The developer enables a server, and the agent uses the tools of that server during a task.
Each developer adds the URLs of the servers to a local configuration file by hand.
An owner selects **Allow all** so that the clients can read the registry.

questions.explanation: The registry must exist before its URL can be entered in the policy, and the policy must be in place before a client can discover the approved servers. The developer then enables a server, and only after that can the agent use its tools. **Allow all** removes the restriction, and manual configuration is the unmanaged discovery that a registry replaces.
questions.takeaway: Registry → policy with the registry URL and Registry only → discovery in the client → use.

evidence.quote: An organization configures an MCP registry
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 3

evidence.quote: The organization defines an allow list policy for approved servers
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 3

evidence.quote: The client discovers approved servers from the registry
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 3

evidence.quote: Registry only → only servers from the registry are allowed
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 3

whyExam.skill: Configure the MCP registries

clues.text: The bullet names the MCP registries.

questions.stem:
An agent opens pull requests in a GitHub repository named Repo1. A ruleset for `main` requires a pull request and a status check named `build`. The ruleset does not require a review. Pull requests that change only files in `docs/` wait an average of one day until a maintainer merges them.

You need to remove the delay for these pull requests. The `build` check must still pass before the changes are merged.

What should you do?

options.text: Enable auto-merge for these pull requests.
options.rationale: Correct. Auto-merge merges a pull request when all required reviews and status checks have passed, so nobody has to wait for the result and merge by hand.

options.text: Add the agent to the bypass list of the ruleset.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A bypass actor can merge without meeting the rules, so `build` would no longer have to pass.

options.text: Remove `build` from the required status checks.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The requirement says that the check must still pass before the changes are merged.

options.text: Require a code owner review for the files in `docs/`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That adds a human approval to low-risk changes and increases the delay.

questions.explanation: Human intervention belongs at decision points, not at every step. For low-risk paths such as `docs/`, the module's autonomy model automates the merge once the required checks pass. Auto-merge does exactly that, and it keeps the control: the pull request is merged only after every requirement of the ruleset is met.
questions.takeaway: Low-risk changes: let auto-merge wait for the required checks. Keep people for the decisions that carry risk.

evidence.quote: merge can be automated using GitHub automerge after required checks (and reviews, if configured) pass
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 6

evidence.quote: Put humans at decision points (merge, deploy, secret access), not at every step (analysis, formatting, routine checks).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 4

evidence.quote: Auto-merge merges a pull request automatically after all required reviews and status checks pass.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Configure human intervention for autonomous agents without slowing delivery

clues.text: The bullet asks for intervention that does not slow delivery, which is the point of this scenario.
M2 unit 6 autonomy table: low-risk paths merge automatically after the required checks.
M6 unit 4 repeats it as a tip: people at decision points, not at every step.

questions.stem:
You delegated a task to GitHub Copilot cloud agent in a GitHub repository named Repo1. The session is associated with pull request #123. No new commit has appeared for 40 minutes, and you suspect that the session is stalled.

You need to stream the session log to your terminal while the agent works. Which command should you run?

options.text: `gh run watch 123`
options.rationale: Incorrect. `gh run watch` follows a workflow run that is identified by its run ID. It does not show the log of an agent session.

options.text: `gh pr checks 123 --watch --interval 30`
options.rationale: Incorrect. This shows the status of the checks of the pull request, not what the agent is doing.

options.text: `gh agent-task list`
options.rationale: Incorrect. This lists your running and past sessions. It does not show a log.

options.text: `gh agent-task view 123 --log --follow`
options.rationale: Correct. `view` selects the session of the pull request, `--log` shows the session log, and `--follow` streams it live.

questions.explanation: A stalled or long-running agent session is diagnosed from its session log. The GitHub CLI can stream that log while the agent works. The log shows the last action of the agent, which tells you whether the agent is waiting, looping or blocked.
questions.takeaway: Stalled agent session → `gh agent-task view … --log --follow`.

evidence.quote: Use this command to debug a stalled or long-running agent run in real time.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 7

evidence.quote: To view the session logs, add the `--log` option. Optionally, use the `--follow` option to stream live logs as the agent works.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Identify failed, partial, or stalled agent executions

clues.text: M4 unit 7 shows the command and says what it is for.
A candidate who passed the live exam (Aug 2026) reported this topic: logs and session history.
Docs describe `--log` and `--follow`.

questions.stem:
An agent's pull request in a GitHub repository named Repo1 implements pagination with a page size of 50. The issue requires a page size of 20. You review the evidence. The issue was updated two weeks ago, but the pull request description still states the earlier value of 50. The agent implemented exactly what the description states, and the workflows ran correctly.

You need to improve the agent's behavior for the next session.

What should you adjust?

options.text: The prompts and instructions, by adding a rule about page sizes to the repository instructions.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The requirement was clear in the issue. A rule in the instructions would be a third copy of a value that belongs to one task.

options.text: The memory and state, by removing the outdated value so that the issue is the single source of truth.
options.rationale: Correct. The failure is a context issue: two artifacts held different values. The fix removes the conflicting copy.

options.text: The tool configuration, by making the validation workflow run on `push` and on `pull_request`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The workflows ran correctly. No test could know which of the two values was intended.

options.text: The tool configuration, by limiting the agent to read-only tools until a reviewer approves the plan.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The agent's tools were not the problem. It followed the information that it was given.

questions.explanation: Classify first, then tune the matching area. The agent used conflicting information across artifacts, which is a context issue. Context issues are fixed in memory and state: update the artifacts with clearer decisions, remove outdated or conflicting context, and keep a single source of truth.
questions.takeaway: Conflicting or stale context → fix memory and state: one source of truth, outdated copies removed.

evidence.quote: Conflicting information across artifacts
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Remove outdated or conflicting context
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Ensure a single source of truth is maintained
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

whyExam.skill: Refine memory usage

clues.text: "Refine memory usage" is a named bullet.
M5 unit 6 names "Memory and state" as one of three areas to adjust, with these actions.

questions.stem:
A workflow in a private GitHub repository named Repo1 has two jobs. The `analyze` job runs an agent that reads the code and produces a report. The `publish` job commits the report to a branch and updates the pull request.

You need to configure the permissions of the `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Each job must have only the permissions that it needs.

How should you complete the workflow?
questions.template:
permissions:
  contents: [[default]]

jobs:
  analyze:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: ./scripts/analyze.sh

  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: analyze
    [[key]]:
      contents: write
      [[scope]]: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: ./scripts/publish.sh

default.rationale: The default for the workflow is read-only. `analyze` inherits it and can check out the code. With `none`, the job could not read the private repository, and with `write`, the agent's job could push.

key.rationale: A `permissions` block on a job replaces the workflow default for that job only.

scope.rationale: Updating a pull request needs `pull-requests: write`. `id-token` is for OIDC tokens, and `security-events` is for code scanning results.

questions.explanation: Least privilege is implemented in two steps: a read-only default at the workflow level, and an elevation only on the job that must write. The job that runs the agent never holds a token that can push. `pull-requests: write` is an elevated capability, so it appears only where the pull request is updated.
questions.takeaway: Read-only default for the workflow. Write permissions only on the job that writes.

evidence.quote: Set a read-only default at the workflow level, then elevate write permissions only for the job that must write.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 5

evidence.quote: Decision guidance: Granting pull-requests: write should be treated as elevated capability. Use it only when the workflow must create/update PRs.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 5

evidence.quote: If you specify the access for any of these permissions, all of those that are not specified are set to `none`.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Scope permissions and execution contexts to enforce least-privilege access

clues.text: The bullet names least-privilege access.
M6 unit 5 shows the workflow default and the job-level elevation in YAML.
A candidate who passed the live exam (Aug 2026) reported this topic: permissions blocks and the scope of `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

questions.stem:
An agent works on a long task in a GitHub repository named Repo1. The pull request description now contains the acceptance criteria, the design decisions, the testing approach, a list of every command that the agent tried, and two older copies of the acceptance criteria. In a new session, the agent implements one of the older copies.

You need to scope the agent's memory to the information that affects the outcome of the task.

What should you do?

options.text: Keep the criteria, the decisions, and the testing approach, and remove the command list and the older copies.
options.rationale: Correct. Requirements, decisions that affect the implementation, and the validation approach are relevant. Intermediate steps and duplicated context are not.

options.text: Move the entire description to a file in the repository, and link the file from the pull request.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The same clutter and the same duplicates would exist in another place.

options.text: Keep everything, and add a note that tells the agent which copy of the criteria is current.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The duplicates remain, and so does the risk that an outdated copy is used.

options.text: Remove the acceptance criteria from the description, and restate them in the prompt of each session.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A prompt is session context. Restating criteria in prompts creates new copies that can diverge.

questions.explanation: Memory should be limited to what affects the outcome: requirements and constraints, decisions that affect the implementation, and the validation approach. Temporary intermediate steps and duplicated context should not be stored. Less memory means less confusion and a lower chance that outdated information is used.
questions.takeaway: Store requirements, decisions and the validation approach. Drop intermediate steps and duplicates.

jobs:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:

questions.stem:
An agent in a GitHub repository named Repo1 rates the risk of its own plans, and low-risk plans are applied automatically. For a plan that contains the following change to `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, the agent reports a low risk, because the diff is one line.

```diff
       - name: Run tests
-        run: dotnet test --no-build
+        run: dotnet test --no-build || true
```

You need to classify the change correctly and apply the matching control.

Which classification and control should you use?

options.text: Low risk: full automation after the required checks pass
options.rationale: Incorrect. The size of a diff says little about its consequence. This line makes the test step succeed even when tests fail.

options.text: Medium risk: a pull request and the required checks
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the control for dependency updates and safe refactoring. The change weakens the very checks that this control relies on.

options.text: High risk: a review by the code owners, explicit approvals, and stronger checks
options.rationale: Correct. Changes to `.github/workflows/` are high risk by default, because they affect the entire pipeline.

options.text: Critical risk: an environment gate with explicit reviewers for each workflow run
options.rationale: Incorrect. The critical level is for production deployments and access to production secrets. An environment gates jobs, not the merge of a change to a workflow file.

questions.explanation: Risk depends on where a change is applied, how easily it can be reversed, and how quickly it affects users or systems. Workflow files, `infra/` and `security/` are "small diff, big consequence" areas and are treated as high risk by default. The matching control is CODEOWNERS with explicit approvals and stronger checks. It also shows why an agent's own rating should not decide the routing for such paths.
questions.takeaway: `.github/workflows/`, `infra/`, `security/` = high risk by default, whatever the size of the diff.

evidence.quote: Treat changes to `.github/workflows/`, `infra/`, and `security/` as high risk by default. These are "small diff, big consequence" areas.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.quote: CODEOWNERS + explicit approvals + stronger checks
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.quote: For example, editing a README file has minimal impact, while modifying `.github/workflows/` affects the entire pipeline.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

questions.stem:
GitHub Copilot cloud agent works on issues in a GitHub repository named Repo1. For some tasks, the agent must read issues in a second repository named Repo2 by using the GitHub MCP server. The agent reports that it cannot access Repo2.

You need to give the agent read access to Repo2 through the GitHub MCP server.

What should you do?

options.text: Add `github.com` to the custom allowlist of the agent's firewall, and start a new agent session.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The network is not what limits the agent. The token that the GitHub MCP server uses can read only Repo1.

options.text: Set `"tools": ["*"]` for the GitHub MCP server in the MCP configuration of Repo1.
options.rationale: Incorrect. `tools` selects which tools of a server the agent may use. It does not change what the server's token can access.

options.text: Configure the GitHub MCP server in the MCP configuration of Repo1, and add an Agents secret named `COPILOT_MCP_GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` that holds a token with read access to Repo2.
options.rationale: Correct. By default, the server uses a token that is scoped to the current repository. A personal access token with wider access, stored under this name, widens what the server can read.

options.text: Add a GitHub Actions secret named `GH_TOKEN` that holds a token with read access to Repo2, and reference the secret in `copilot-setup-steps.yml`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The agent cannot read secrets that were created for GitHub Actions, and `GH_TOKEN` is not the name that the GitHub MCP server looks for.

questions.explanation: The GitHub MCP server is built into the cloud agent. By default it connects with a specially scoped token that has read-only access to the current repository. To reach data outside that repository, you configure the server with a personal access token that has wider access, or with a GitHub App. GitHub recommends a fine-grained token that is limited to read-only permissions on the repositories that the agent needs.

To allow Copilot to access data outside the current repository, you can configure a personal access token with wider access or a GitHub App. For a personal access token, you add a secret called `COPILOT_MCP_GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN`.

options.text: The scope, which states what will change.
options.rationale: Correct. A reviewer can compare the scope with the files that the pull request changes.

options.text: The agent's confidence score for the change.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Evaluation is grounded in system signals, not in the agent's confidence.

options.text: The success criteria, which state how the result will be verified.
options.rationale: Correct. Without them, nobody can tell whether the plan worked.

options.text: The full transcript of the agent session.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A transcript is raw material. A plan is a structured artifact that a reviewer can assess quickly.

options.text: A rollback or escalation path.
options.rationale: Correct. It says what happens if the change fails or if the agent cannot finish.

options.text: The name of the model that the agent used.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The model name does not make the approach easier to review.

questions.takeaway: A reviewable plan states scope, success criteria, and a rollback or escalation path.

questions.stem:
In a GitHub repository named Repo1, a security agent and a dependency agent each open a pull request for the same code scanning alert. One pull request upgrades the affected library, and the other replaces the library. Both pull requests pass the required checks, and the two fixes cannot be combined.

You need to resolve the situation in a predictable way. What should occur next?

options.text: The pull request that passed its checks first is merged, and the other one is closed.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The outcome would be decided by timing, not by correctness.

options.text: Both agents rebase their branches until one of the pull requests has no conflicts.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The fixes are incompatible by design. More automated attempts cannot decide between them.

options.text: Automation stops, and a human receives a short report of the conflict, the attempts, and the options.
options.rationale: Correct. Two incompatible fixes for the same alert are an escalation threshold. A person decides, with the facts in hand.

options.text: Both pull requests are merged, and the resulting conflict is resolved on `main`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That moves the conflict into the protected branch, where it affects everyone.

questions.explanation: This is duplicate effort that ended in contradictory outputs. The module defines escalation thresholds so that automation stops before it creates instability: a pull request that conflicts twice after rebasing, a required check that fails twice with the same signature, or two agents that propose incompatible fixes to the same alert. The escalation includes a short report.

evidence.quote: if two agents propose incompatible fixes to the same alert.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 5

evidence.quote: Escalation should include a short report: what conflicted, what was attempted, and which options exist.

questions.stem:
A product owner creates the following issue in a GitHub repository named Repo1 and plans to assign it to GitHub Copilot cloud agent.

```text
Title: Make the checkout API faster
Body: Customers complain. Please improve performance.
```

You need to ensure that the result of the task can be evaluated.

What should you do first?

options.text: Assign the issue to the agent, and evaluate the result by confirming that the required checks pass.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The checks show that nothing broke. They cannot show whether the API is fast enough, because nobody said what that means.

options.text: Assign the issue to the agent, and ask the agent to define its own acceptance criteria.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The agent would then judge its work by criteria that it chose itself.

options.text: Add acceptance criteria, constraints, the paths in scope, and the expected validation to the issue.
options.rationale: Correct. A task is ready for an agent when the expected outcome and its limits are defined precisely.

options.text: Add a required status check named `performance` to the ruleset for `main`.

options.text: Formatting code

targets.text: The workflow outputs that record the results of validation

- **Goal:**
- **Scope (paths/files):**
- **Success criteria (verifiable):**

You need to guarantee that a pull request cannot be merged into `main` unless it contains a plan.

What should you do?

options.rationale: Incorrect. A comment is a process expectation. Nothing stops a pull request that ignores it.

options.text: Add a workflow that fails when the plan is missing, and require its status check.
options.rationale: Correct. A required status check turns the expectation into a condition that the platform enforces before merging.

options.text: Add an instruction to the custom instructions of Repo1 to complete the Plan section.
options.rationale: Incorrect. An instruction guides the agent. It does not block a pull request in which the agent did not follow it.

options.text: Increase the number of required approving reviews in the ruleset to two.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Reviewers already approve pull requests without a plan. A second approval does not check for one.

questions.explanation: A template asks for a plan, and a required status check enforces it. A workflow that fails when the plan is missing, selected as a required check in the ruleset, means that the pull request cannot be merged until the plan exists.
questions.takeaway: Template = expectation. Required status check = guarantee.

evidence.quote: In addition to templates, you can enforce plan gating as a required status check. This turns a process expectation ("include a plan") into a system guarantee.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 5

evidence.quote: A repository administrator can mark Plan Gate as a required status check using rulesets/branch protection, ensuring PRs can't merge unless the plan exists.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 5

whyExam.skill: Validate agent plans

clues.text: M2 unit 5: a required status check turns "include a plan" into a system guarantee.
Guidance versus enforcement recurs in M2 unit 4, M2 unit 7 and M6 unit 3.
A template and an instruction both look like controls. Neither blocks a merge.

questions.stem:
The agents in a GitHub repository named Repo1 use a pull request structure that has the following sections.

```md
## Objective
## Plan
## Evidence
## Decisions and handoffs
## Risks and rollback
```

Which section should contain each item?

targets.text: The link to the CI run and the scan outputs
targets.rationale: Runs and scan outputs are what a reviewer inspects to verify the result.

targets.text: The next owner when an escalation is needed
targets.rationale: A handoff names who continues. It is recorded with the decision that led to it.

targets.text: The problem that the pull request solves
targets.rationale: The objective states the problem, before any step is described.

targets.text: The rationale for choosing one approach over another
targets.rationale: A decision is recorded together with its rationale, so that a later agent or reviewer does not reopen it.

questions.explanation: A standard structure keeps handoffs consistent across agents. The objective states the problem, the plan lists the steps, the evidence links the CI run, the scan outputs and the related issue or alert, the decisions and handoffs section records each decision with its rationale and the next owner, and the last section holds the risks and the rollback.
questions.takeaway: Decision, rationale and next owner go in Decisions and handoffs. Runs and scans go in Evidence.

evidence.quote: What problem is being solved?
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 6

evidence.quote: Next owner (if escalation needed):
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 6

evidence.quote: Rationale:
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 6

evidence.quote: This structure ensures that every decision is captured, every action is justified, and every handoff is clear.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 6

whyExam.skill: Document key decisions, handoffs, and outcomes across agents

questions.stem:
You are selecting the signals that are used to evaluate the work of agents in a GitHub repository named Repo1.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

items.statement: Review feedback, such as requested changes and approvals, is an evaluation signal.
items.explanation: Code review feedback is one of the common evaluation signals. It carries the human judgment that checks cannot give.

items.statement: Code scanning results and secret scanning alerts are evaluation signals for security-oriented work.
items.explanation: Security signals are part of evaluation, next to workflow runs and review feedback.

items.statement: When a pull request has no workflow run, the agent's statement that the tests passed is sufficient evidence.
items.explanation: Evaluation is grounded in system signals, not in the agent's confidence. A missing run is a missing signal.

questions.explanation: The module names three groups of signals: workflow runs and status checks, code review feedback, and security signals. The first and the third are measured by the system, and review feedback is a judgment by a person. What is never a signal is the agent's own account of its work.
questions.takeaway: Signals come from the system and from reviewers: checks, review feedback, security results. Never from the agent's confidence.

evidence.quote: Code review feedback (requested changes, approvals)
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M1, unit 3

evidence.quote: Security signals (code scanning results, secret scanning alerts, dependency alerts)
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M1, unit 3

evidence.quote: These capabilities reinforce a key lesson: agent evaluation must be grounded in system signals, not in the agent's confidence.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M1, unit 3

whyExam.skill: Identify qualitative and quantitative evaluation signals to evaluate agents

questions.stem:
A workflow in a GitHub repository named Repo1 deploys to an environment named `production`. The environment has three required reviewers. An audit finds that one of the required reviewers started a deployment of an agent's change and then approved the same deployment.

You need to ensure that the user who starts a deployment cannot approve it. What should you do?

options.text: Add a wait timer of 30 minutes to the `production` environment.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A wait timer delays the job. It does not change who may approve it.

options.text: Select **Prevent self-review** for the `production` environment.
options.rationale: Correct. With this setting, a user who initiates a deployment cannot approve the deployment job, even as a required reviewer.

options.text: Increase the number of required reviewers of the environment to six.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Only one of the required reviewers needs to approve a job, and that one can still be the user who started it.

options.text: Limit the deployment branches of the environment to `main`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That restricts which branches can deploy. It says nothing about who approves.

questions.explanation: A production approval must be explicit, auditable and owned by an accountable role. An approval by the person who started the deployment is not an independent decision. Environments have a setting for this case: with self-review prevented, a deployment to a protected environment is always reviewed by a second person.
questions.takeaway: Independent production approval → **Prevent self-review** on the environment.

evidence.quote: Decision guidance: Production approvals should be explicit, auditable, and owned by accountable roles.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 4

evidence.quote: If you enable this setting, users who initiate a deployment cannot approve the deployment job, even if they are a required reviewer.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

evidence.quote: Only one of the required reviewers needs to approve the job for it to proceed.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Require explicit authorization or controlled paths for irreversible or compliance-sensitive changes

clues.text: The bullet names explicit authorization.
Docs define **Prevent self-review** and state that one approval is enough.

questions.stem:
An agent's pull request in a GitHub repository named Repo1 has more than 100 comments, many of which contain pasted logs. The requirements and the approach have not changed. New agent sessions overlook the final decisions, which are spread over the comments.

You need to keep the history manageable and preserve traceability.

What should you do?

options.text: Close the pull request, and open a new pull request for the same branch.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is a reset, which is used when the requirements or the approach change. Nothing changed here.

options.text: Delete the workflow runs and the artifacts that the pasted logs came from.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is pruning of evidence that is still needed, and deleted artifacts cannot be restored.

options.text: Update the description with the final decisions, and link to the workflow runs instead of pasting logs.
options.rationale: Correct. This is summarization: the description carries the decisions, and links keep the full evidence reachable.

options.text: Increase the retention period for workflow logs and artifacts in Repo1.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Retention decides how long evidence is kept. It does not make the decisions easier to find.

questions.explanation: The module names four ways to maintain memory: expiration, pruning, summarization and reset. When the detailed history is too long but still valid, the answer is summarization. The pull request description holds the final decisions, key commits are referenced, and workflow runs are linked, not copied.
questions.takeaway: Long but valid history → summarize in the description and link to the evidence.

evidence.quote: Update the pull request description with final decisions
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 3

evidence.quote: Link to workflow runs instead of storing full logs
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 3

evidence.quote: This preserves traceability while keeping memory manageable.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 3

whyExam.skill: Define memory expiration, pruning, and reset rules

clues.text: The bullet names expiration, pruning and reset.
M5 unit 3 has a subsection for each of expiration, pruning, summarization and reset.
Reset and pruning are the neighboring concepts that look like a cleanup.

questions.stem:
A GitHub organization named Org1 has 40 repositories. GitHub Copilot cloud agent is enabled for the members of Org1 and is available in every repository.

You need to ensure that the agent can be used only in two repositories named Repo1 and Repo2. The members must keep their access to the other features of Copilot.

What should you do?

options.text: In the settings of Org1, set the repository access of the cloud agent to **Selected repositories**, and select Repo1 and Repo2.
options.rationale: Correct. The "Repository access" control defines which repositories allow the agent. The other Copilot features are not affected.

options.text: In the Copilot policies of Org1, disable the policy for the cloud agent.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That blocks the agent in all 40 repositories, including Repo1 and Repo2.

options.text: In each of the other repositories, add a ruleset that blocks branches whose names start with `copilot/`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That only makes the agent's sessions fail in 38 repositories. It does not scope where the agent is available, and it must be maintained for every new repository.

options.text: In Repo1 and Repo2, add a custom agent profile that sets the `target` property to the repository name.
options.rationale: Incorrect. `target` selects the environment of a custom agent, such as `vscode` or `github-copilot`. It does not limit repositories.

questions.explanation: Repository scope is the first boundary of an agent's execution context. By default, the cloud agent is available in all repositories of an organization in which it is enabled. An organization owner narrows this with the "Repository access" control. In a repository where the agent is available, any user who has access to Copilot and write permission can delegate work to it.
questions.takeaway: Scope the cloud agent with Repository access → Selected repositories in the organization settings.

evidence.quote: Repository scope is the first boundary that limits agent behavior.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 4

evidence.quote: Use the "Repository access" control to define which repositories allow the agent.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

evidence.note: By default, the cloud agent is available in all repositories in an organization where it is enabled. An organization owner can block the agent from being used in some or all repositories, for example by choosing "Selected repositories".
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Configure an agent's scope to a specific repository

clues.text: The bullet names the scope to a specific repository.
M3 unit 4 calls repository scope the first boundary and shows where it is configured.
Docs name the control: Repository access, with Selected repositories.

questions.stem:
You are reviewing how agents work in a GitHub organization named Org1, and you find three anti-patterns.

Which mitigation should you use for each anti-pattern?

choices.text: A pull request template that has a required plan section, and a review before merging
A least-privilege `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and environments that have required reviewers
CODEOWNERS, required reviews, and risk-based approvals in addition to the checks
A longer retention period for workflow logs

targets.text: The workflow that runs an agent can write to the repository and can read every secret.
targets.rationale: This is an over-permissioned agent. The mitigation reduces what the token can do and puts secrets behind an approval.

targets.text: Pull requests are merged as soon as CI passes, because passing checks are taken as proof that a change is appropriate.
targets.rationale: This is blind trust in automation. Checks only validate what they are designed to detect, so human review by the right owners is added.

targets.text: Agents begin to change code without a visible approach.
targets.rationale: This is planless execution. The template makes the plan part of every pull request, and the review reads it.

questions.explanation: The module maps each anti-pattern to GitHub controls. Over-permissioned agents are answered with a least-privilege token and environments. Blind trust in automation is answered by combining checks with CODEOWNERS, required reviews and risk-based approvals. Planless execution is answered with a plan section in the pull request template. Longer log retention mitigates none of the three.
questions.takeaway: Over-permissioned → least privilege and environments. Blind trust → reviews next to checks. Planless → plan section in the template.

evidence.quote: Over-permissioned agents: The agent (or its workflow token/tooling credentials) has broader access than necessary.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M1, unit 5

evidence.quote: Blind trust in automation: Passing CI matters, but checks only validate what they're designed to detect.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M1, unit 5

evidence.quote: Combine checks with CODEOWNERS, required reviews, and risk-based approvals
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M1, unit 5

evidence.quote: Require a plan section via PR template; require review before merge
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M1, unit 5

whyExam.skill: Identify and mitigate common anti-patterns in agents

clues.text: The bullet asks to identify and to mitigate, which is the shape of this item.
M1 unit 5 has a table that maps each anti-pattern to GitHub controls.

questions.stem:
A GitHub repository named Repo1 has a dependency agent and a refactoring agent. Each agent has its own workflow and its own branch prefix. You plan to add a test agent that writes unit tests in `tests/`.

You need to add the test agent without creating interference with the existing agents. Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Give the test agent a dedicated branch prefix, such as `agent/test/<ticket>`.
options.rationale: Correct. A branch for each agent keeps its changes bounded and its ownership clear.

options.text: Let the test agent push its commits to the open branches of the refactoring agent.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Shared branches interleave commits and make ownership, rollback and auditing harder.

options.text: Give the test agent a dedicated workflow that has only the permissions that the agent needs.
options.rationale: Correct. Separate workflows keep triggers, permissions and outputs easy to reason about.

options.text: Reuse the workflow of the dependency agent, and add the permissions that the test agent needs.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That couples the two agents and widens the permissions of both.

options.text: Allow the test agent to change `src/` so that it can fix the code that its tests cover.
options.rationale: Incorrect. `src/` is the scope of the refactoring agent. Overlapping scopes produce collisions.

questions.explanation: A new agent joins an existing system through the same isolation rules as the others: a narrow role, a scope that is limited by path, a dedicated branch, and a dedicated workflow or job with its own minimal permissions. Each of these prevents one kind of interference: overlapping changes, interleaved commits, or shared permissions.
questions.takeaway: New agent: its own role, paths, branch prefix, and workflow with minimal permissions.

evidence.quote: Each agent should open a PR from a dedicated branch such as:
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 4

evidence.quote: Give each agent a dedicated workflow (or a dedicated job with distinct permissions) so triggers, permissions, and outputs are easy to reason about.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 4

evidence.quote: A strong design prevents these outcomes by assigning each agent a narrow role, limiting scope by path and artifact type, and defining completion signals that can be verified through GitHub checks and review outcomes.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 2

whyExam.skill: Add agents to existing multi-agent workflows

clues.text: The bullet names adding agents.
M4 unit 4 describes branch, workflow and permission isolation for each agent.
M4 unit 2 defines scope boundaries by path.

questions.stem:
In a .NET repository named Repo1, an agent's pull requests often fail the `build` check on the first attempt. You review the session logs of five failed tasks. In each task, the agent ran `npm test`, although Repo1 contains no Node.js project, and then reported that validation was complete. The issues were clear, the pull request descriptions were consistent with the issues, and the `build` workflow reported the failures correctly.

You need to improve the agent's behavior. What should you do?

options.text: Add the build and test commands of Repo1 to the custom instructions of the repository.
options.rationale: Correct. The agent does not know how this repository is validated. Repository instructions give it that expectation in every session.

options.text: Rewrite the acceptance criteria of the five issues, and assign the issues again.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The issues were clear. The same wrong command would be used again.

options.text: Remove `build` from the required status checks until the agent is more reliable.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The check is the control that caught the failures. Removing it hides the problem and lets broken changes merge.

options.text: Change the `build` workflow so that it runs `npm test` before `dotnet test`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That adapts the validation to the agent's mistake. The workflow already reports the correct result.

questions.explanation: The logs show a repeated incorrect command, while the task definitions and the workflow are sound. The area to tune is prompts and instructions: add the expectation that is missing, here the commands that build and test the repository, to the repository instruction files. The required check stays in place to verify the improvement.
questions.takeaway: Agent repeats a wrong command → state the right commands in the repository instructions. Never weaken the check.

evidence.quote: Incorrect commands or scripts
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Improve clarity and specificity in prompts or repository instructions.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Update repository instruction files
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

whyExam.skill: Revise instructions, workflows, or constraints

clues.text: The bullet names the revision of instructions.
M5 unit 6 names "Prompts and instructions" as an area to adjust, with repository instruction files.
Weakening the check or the workflow makes the symptom disappear.

questions.stem:
A workflow in a GitHub repository named Repo1 contains the following steps.

```yaml
- name: Run agent task
  run: copilot -p "Update the API reference in docs/" --no-ask-user
  continue-on-error: true
- name: Open pull request
  run: ./scripts/open-pr.sh
```

Last night, the agent step failed halfway, and the workflow opened a pull request that contained incomplete changes.

You need to ensure that the job stops when the agent step fails. What should you do?

options.text: Add `if: always()` to the `Open pull request` step.
options.rationale: Incorrect. `always()` makes the step run even after a failure, which is the opposite of what is required.

options.text: Add `timeout-minutes: 10` to the `Run agent task` step.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A timeout limits how long the step may run. With `continue-on-error: true`, the job still continues after the step fails.

options.text: Set `fail-fast: false` in the `strategy` of the job.
options.rationale: Incorrect. `fail-fast` controls whether the other jobs of a matrix are canceled. It does not affect the steps of this job.

options.text: Remove `continue-on-error: true` from the `Run agent task` step.
options.rationale: Correct. Without it, a failed step fails the job, and the later steps do not run.

questions.explanation: Error handling starts with failing fast. `continue-on-error: true` lets a job pass when the step fails, so the next step ran on a half-finished result. Without the setting, the default applies: the job stops at the failed step, and no partial change reaches a pull request.
questions.takeaway: Agent steps must fail fast. `continue-on-error: true` turns an error into a silent continuation.

evidence.quote: This ensures that errors stop execution instead of silently continuing.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 5

evidence.quote: Preventing partial or inconsistent changes
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 5

evidence.quote: Prevents a job from failing when a step fails. Set to `true` to allow a job to pass when this step fails.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Implement error handling

clues.text: "Implement error handling" is a named bullet.
M3 unit 5 shows `continue-on-error: false` on the agent step.
Docs define what `continue-on-error: true` does to the job.

questions.stem:
You are separating planning from execution for the agents in a GitHub repository named Repo1.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

items.statement: In a plan and execution workflow, code changes can be merged before the plan has been validated.
items.explanation: Code is generated immediately, but validation is still required before the merge. The GitHub controls are the same as in a plan-first workflow.

items.statement: A deliberate handoff to an implementation agent after the plan is approved keeps execution from starting during planning.
items.explanation: An explicit transition is one of the ways to enforce the boundary: execution occurs only after the plan is approved.

items.statement: In an automated orchestration, planning can run without tool execution, and the tools can be enabled only after the plan is accepted.
items.explanation: This is tool gating in an orchestrator. The plan is produced first, and tools become available afterwards.

questions.explanation: The two workflows differ in when code is generated, not in whether it is validated. In both, nothing merges before the checks and the reviews pass. The boundary between planning and execution is enforced with capability limits: read-only planning agents, an explicit handoff, tool gating in orchestrators, and plan modes that pause before changes are applied.
questions.takeaway: Both workflows validate before merge. Handoffs and tool gating enforce the planning boundary.

evidence.quote: Option B (Plan + execution): Code is generated immediately, but validation is still required before merge.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 4

evidence.quote: Execution should occur only after plan approval, using a deliberate handoff.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 4

evidence.quote: you can force planning to run without tool execution and then enable tools only after the plan is accepted.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 4

whyExam.skill: Prevent agent action until the agent checked and approved

clues.text: M2 unit 4 lists four ways to enforce the planning boundary, including handoff and tool gating.
Plan and execution is often misread as "no validation". Validation is still required before merge.

questions.stem:
A GitHub repository named Repo1 has a documentation agent that is defined by an agent profile and a dedicated workflow. The agent has two open pull requests and many merged pull requests. The team decides to retire the agent. Auditors must still be able to reconstruct what the agent did, and the other agents must continue to work.

You need to retire the agent. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the agent profile and the workflow in a reviewed pull request, and assign an owner to the two open pull requests.
options.rationale: Correct. The retirement itself leaves a trace, the history of the agent stays in the repository, and the unfinished work gets a clear owner.

options.text: Delete the agent's branches, workflow runs, and artifacts, and then remove the agent profile.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That destroys the evidence that the auditors need, and deleted artifacts cannot be restored.

options.text: Set `user-invocable: false` in the agent profile, and leave the workflow enabled.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The agent can then no longer be selected by a user, but it can still be accessed programmatically, and its workflow keeps running. It is hidden, not retired.

options.text: Remove the agent profile by pushing directly to `main`, and close the open pull requests without a comment.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A direct push bypasses review, and pull requests that are closed without a reason leave the outcome of the work unclear.

questions.explanation: Retirement is the last stage of the agent lifecycle, and it follows the same rules as every other change: it goes through a pull request, it leaves a durable trace, and ownership is explicit. The merged pull requests, the workflow runs and the Git history remain as the audit trail. The module names the lifecycle stages but gives no procedure, so this answer applies its principles.
questions.takeaway: Retire an agent through a reviewed pull request, keep its history, and give its open work an owner.

evidence.quote: Agent lifecycle management follows a continuous sequence of deployment, monitoring, updating, and eventual retirement.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 7

evidence.quote: A practical observability goal is that every meaningful step leaves a durable trace in GitHub:
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 6

evidence.quote: When `false`, the agent cannot be manually selected and can only be accessed programmatically.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Retire agents while preserving auditability and workflow continuity

clues.text: The bullet names retirement, auditability and continuity. Learn mentions retirement in one sentence only, so an exam item must rest on the general principles used here.

options.text: A context issue, because the agent used stale information
options.rationale: Incorrect. The issue and the pull request description agree, so the agent had the correct and current information.

options.text: Tool misuse, because the test workflow is misconfigured
options.rationale: Incorrect. The workflow ran the complete test suite. It reported what the changed test asserts, which is nothing.

options.text: A reasoning error, because the agent ignored the acceptance criteria
options.rationale: Correct. The agent made the test pass by removing the assertion. It chose an invalid way to reach a green check.

options.text: An environment issue, because the runner lacks a dependency
options.rationale: Incorrect. Nothing failed to run. The checks passed.

questions.explanation: Compare intent with result. The intent is a correct total, verified by the test. The result is a test that no longer verifies anything. The information was complete and the tools worked, so the cause is a reasoning error: an incorrect decision that ignores the acceptance criteria. It also shows why passing checks are not proof that a change is appropriate.
questions.takeaway: Right information, working tools, wrong decision → reasoning error.

evidence.quote: Incorrect assumptions or decisions that lead to invalid changes.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Ignoring acceptance criteria
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Missing, stale, or conflicting information that leads to incorrect behavior.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

whyExam.skill: Classify root causes, including reasoning errors, tool misuse, and context or environment issues

clues.text: The bullet lists the categories by name.
M5 unit 6 defines each category with examples.
All checks pass, which hides the failure.

questions.stem:
A workflow in a GitHub repository named Repo1 validates the pull requests of an agent. The workflow has the following requirements:

- The `validate` job must run only when the run was triggered by a pull request.
- The build configuration must come from a repository variable named `BUILD_CONFIGURATION` that is managed in the settings of Repo1.
- The test step must use the verbosity that the job sets in an environment variable named `TEST_VERBOSITY`.

You need to use the correct context for each value.

How should you complete the workflow?
questions.template:
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  validate:
    if: [[event]].event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      TEST_VERBOSITY: minimal
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: dotnet build --configuration ${{ [[config]].BUILD_CONFIGURATION }}
      - run: dotnet test --verbosity ${{ [[level]].TEST_VERBOSITY }}

event.rationale: The `github` context holds information about the workflow run, including the event that triggered it.

config.rationale: The `vars` context contains the configuration variables that are set at the repository, organization, or environment level.

level.rationale: The `env` context contains the variables that are set in the workflow, the job, or the step. `TEST_VERBOSITY` is set on the job.

questions.explanation: Each context has one purpose. `github` answers what triggered the run and is used for runtime decisions such as defensive gating. `vars` holds configuration that is managed centrally and reused. `env` holds the variables that the workflow itself defines. `secrets` is for sensitive values, and none of the three values is one.
questions.takeaway: `github` = the event and the run. `vars` = managed configuration. `env` = variables set in the workflow.

evidence.quote: github.* → event metadata and runtime decisions ("what triggered this run?")
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 6

evidence.quote: vars.* → centrally managed configuration values designed to be reused
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 6

evidence.quote: env.* → job-level environment variables and runtime configuration
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 6

evidence.quote: Contains variables set at the repository, organization, or environment levels.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Configure an agent to be invoked in a CI workflow

clues.text: M2 unit 6 has a section named "Contexts: GitHub vs vars vs env" with one line for each.
The unit shows `github.event_name` in a job condition.

questions.stem:
A dependency remediation agent in a GitHub repository named Repo1 is scoped to the implementation stage of the SDLC. The agent detects a vulnerable dependency, creates a branch, and updates the dependency and the lock file.

You need to define the last step that the agent performs before its scoped responsibility is complete. Which step should you define?

options.text: The agent merges the branch into `main` after the required checks pass.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Acceptance belongs to the reviewers and to repository policy, not to the agent.

options.text: The agent approves the pull request on behalf of the security team.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Approval is human judgment. An agent that approves its own work removes the boundary.

options.text: The agent opens a pull request that includes a structured plan and the expected success signals.
options.rationale: Correct. With the pull request, the implementation stage ends. Validation and acceptance happen through checks, reviews and policy.

options.text: The agent deploys the fix to production and verifies the result.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Deployment is the stage that is usually restricted for agents and gated by approvals.
