questions.stem:
A custom agent named `implementer` is defined by an agent profile on the `main` branch of a GitHub repository named Repo1. The agent created three pull requests that are still open, and reviewers continue to interact with the agent in those pull requests. You merge a change to the agent profile that removes the `execute` tool.

You need to plan the rollout of the change. Which behavior should you expect?

options.text: All sessions, including the interactions in the three open pull requests, use the updated profile immediately.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The interactions in a pull request keep the version of the agent that created the pull request.

options.text: The three open pull requests are closed, because the version of the agent that created them no longer exists.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Updating a profile does not close pull requests. Every version remains in the Git history.

options.text: The updated profile is used only after the agent is removed and added again in the settings of Repo1.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The profile is a file in the repository. A new task picks up its latest version without any other step.

options.text: New tasks use the updated profile, and the interactions in the three open pull requests keep the earlier version.
options.rationale: Correct. The version of a custom agent is the commit SHA of its profile. A new task uses the latest version, and a pull request stays with the version that created it.

questions.explanation: Custom agents are versioned by the Git commit SHA of the agent profile. A task that is assigned to the agent uses the latest version of the profile for that repository and branch. Interactions within a pull request that the agent created keep the same version, for consistency. An update therefore does not disrupt active work, and it also does not reach it: to apply the stricter tools to the open pull requests, start new tasks.
questions.takeaway: Agent profile update: new tasks get it, open pull requests keep the version that created them.

evidence.quote: Agent lifecycle management follows a continuous sequence of deployment, monitoring, updating, and eventual retirement.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 7

evidence.note: Custom agent versioning is based on Git commit SHAs for the agent profile file. When you assign a custom agent to a task, the agent is instantiated using the latest version of the agent profile for that repository and branch. When the agent creates a pull request, interactions within the pull request use the same version of the custom agent for consistency.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Update, reconfigure, or replace agents without disrupting active workflows

clues.text: The bullet names updates that do not disrupt active work.
Docs define how agent profiles are versioned and which version an open pull request uses.

questions.stem:
A custom agent updates the Markdown documentation in a GitHub repository named Repo1. The agent profile starts with the following frontmatter.

```yaml
---
name: docs-writer
description: Updates the Markdown documentation
---
```

You analyze a failed task. The agent ran a formatter from the shell, and the formatter rewrote 400 source files. To do its work, the agent must read, search, and edit files. It never needs to run commands.

You need to refine the agent's tool access so that the failure cannot recur.

What should you do?

options.text: Add a sentence to the agent profile that forbids the use of formatters.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A sentence in the profile is guidance. The shell tool would still be available.

options.text: Set the `tools` property of the agent profile to `read`, `edit`, and `search`.
options.rationale: Correct. A specific list enables only those tools. Without `execute`, the agent cannot run a command.

options.text: Set the `tools` property of the agent profile to an empty list.
options.rationale: Incorrect. An empty list disables all tools, so the agent could no longer read or edit the documentation.

options.text: Set `disable-model-invocation: true` in the agent profile.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That controls whether the agent is selected automatically. It does not change which tools the agent has.

questions.explanation: The profile has no `tools` property, and an omitted property enables every tool, including the shell. The failure is a tool misuse that the configuration allowed. Tuning the tool access means an allowlist that matches the task: `read`, `search` and `edit` for a documentation agent. An instruction would leave the capability in place.
questions.takeaway: No `tools` property = all tools. Refine tool access with an allowlist that matches the task.

evidence.quote: Incorrect use of workflows, commands, or repository operations.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Capability boundary: which tools are allowed (prefer allowlists)
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.quote: If no tools are specified, all available tools are enabled
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

evidence.quote: An empty tools list (`tools: []`) disables all tools
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Refine tool usage and tool access

clues.text: The bullet names tool access.
Docs: an agent profile without `tools` enables all tools.
Allowlists for tools appear in M2 unit 4 and M2 unit 7.

questions.stem:
A GitHub repository named Repo1 has a default branch named `main` and a maintenance branch named `release/2.4`. You delegate a bug fix for version 2.4 to GitHub Copilot cloud agent from the GitHub CLI.

You need to ensure that the agent creates its working branch from `release/2.4` and not from `main`.

Which command should you run?

options.text: `gh agent-task create "Fix the rounding error in invoice totals" --base release/2.4`
options.rationale: Correct. `--base` chooses a base branch for the task, instead of the default branch of the repository.

options.text: `gh agent-task create "Fix the rounding error in invoice totals" --repo release/2.4`
options.rationale: Incorrect. `--repo` selects a repository, not a branch.

options.text: `gh agent-task create "Fix the rounding error in invoice totals on release/2.4" --follow`
options.rationale: Incorrect. `--follow` streams the session log. Naming the branch in the prompt is guidance, and the task still starts from the default branch.

options.text: `gh agent-task view release/2.4 --log`
options.rationale: Incorrect. `view` shows an existing session. It does not start a task.

questions.explanation: Branch-based scope is set by the system that runs the agent, not by the agent's own configuration. When you delegate a task, you can select the base branch. The agent then creates its working branch from that branch and opens a pull request that targets it. From the GitHub CLI, the option is `--base`.
questions.takeaway: Base branch for an agent task: select it when you delegate. In the CLI, `gh agent-task create … --base BRANCH`.

evidence.quote: When delegating tasks to the Copilot coding agent, you can select a specific base branch.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 4

evidence.quote: Branch-based scope is always enforced by the execution context, not the custom agent itself.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 4

evidence.quote: Choose a base branch, instead of using the repository's default branch (`--base`)
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

questions.stem:
Reviewers in a GitHub repository named Repo1 accept an agent's pull request when all checks pass and the agent's final comment states that the task is complete. Several accepted pull requests did not solve the problem that the issue described.

You need to align the evaluation with the intent of each task. Which comparison should you use?

options.text: The agent's final comment with the plan in the pull request description
options.rationale: Incorrect. Both are the agent's own account. Neither shows what was produced.

options.text: The diff of the pull request with the diff of a similar pull request that was merged
options.rationale: Incorrect. Another pull request does not define what this task was expected to achieve.

options.text: The check results of the pull request with the check results of the previous run
options.rationale: Incorrect. That shows a regression between runs. It does not show whether the requirement is met.

options.text: The acceptance criteria in the issue with the commits and the workflow results
options.rationale: Correct. Intent is captured in the issue. Results are captured in the commits and the workflow outputs.

questions.explanation: To judge whether a task met its intent, compare what the agent was expected to do with what was produced. Intent lives in the issue description and in the plan of the pull request. Results live in the commits, the code changes and the workflow outputs. A statement by the agent that the task is complete is neither.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate intent against results: acceptance criteria versus commits and workflow outputs.

evidence.quote: To understand a failure, compare what the agent was expected to do with what was produced.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Issue descriptions (requirements and acceptance criteria)
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Commits and code changes
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Workflow outputs and logs
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

whyExam.skill: Align evaluation criteria with development intent

clues.text: The bullet names development intent.
M5 unit 6 has a section "Compare intent with results".

questions.stem:
A scheduled workflow in a GitHub repository named Repo1 runs an agent task. About one run in ten fails, because the package registry returns a temporary network error. The same run succeeds when a maintainer starts it again.

You need to ensure that the workflow recovers from this failure without manual intervention. The workflow must not loop indefinitely, and a failure that persists must remain visible.

What should you do?

options.text: Set `continue-on-error: true` on the step that runs the agent task.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The job would pass whether the task succeeded or not, so a persistent failure would be hidden.

options.text: Run the step in a loop of at most three attempts, and fail the step if every attempt fails.
options.rationale: Correct. A bounded retry absorbs a transient error, and the final failure keeps a persistent problem visible.

options.text: Add a second workflow that starts the first workflow again each time that it fails.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Nothing limits the number of restarts, so a persistent failure would loop indefinitely.

options.text: Assign every failed run to a maintainer, who investigates it before a new attempt.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is manual intervention for a failure that a retry resolves.

questions.explanation: Retries are for temporary failures, such as network issues. They must be bounded, and the last attempt must still be able to fail. A retry loop that ends without an error after the final attempt reports success for a run that failed. Escalation to a person is the next stage, for failures that repeat.
questions.takeaway: Transient failure → bounded retry that still fails at the end. Repeated failure → escalation.

evidence.quote: Retries help handle temporary failures such as network issues or transient errors.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 5

evidence.quote: Using retry logic in scripts
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 5

evidence.quote: Bounded retries for transient failures
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.quote: This policy helps prevent infinite loops and makes failures actionable.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

whyExam.skill: Implement retries

clues.text: "Implement retries" is a named bullet.
M3 unit 5 shows a retry loop of three attempts.
Bounded retries return in M2 unit 7, M4 unit 7 and M6 unit 7.

questions.stem:
An owner of a GitHub organization named Org1 configures a custom MCP registry and selects **Registry only** to restrict MCP access. In Visual Studio Code, developers can now use only the servers that the registry lists. An audit finds that GitHub Copilot cloud agent in a repository named Repo1 still uses an MCP server that the registry does not list. The server is defined in the MCP configuration of Repo1.

You need to explain the audit finding. What is the cause?

options.text: The policy applies to remote MCP servers only, and the server in Repo1 is a local server.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Under **Registry only**, the enforcement applies to both remote and local MCP servers.

options.text: A change of the policy is applied to the cloud agent only after 24 hours.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A selected policy is applied immediately. Waiting does not change the finding.

options.text: MCP private registry enforcement is not supported for GitHub Copilot cloud agent.
options.rationale: Correct. The reference lists the supported surfaces. Copilot CLI and the IDEs are supported, and the cloud agent is not.

options.text: The server sets `"tools": ["*"]`, which exempts the server from the policy.
options.rationale: Incorrect. `tools` selects the tools of a server that the agent may use. It has no effect on the registry policy.

questions.explanation: The registry policy governs the Copilot clients that developers use: the IDEs and Copilot CLI. The cloud agent takes its MCP servers from the MCP configuration of the repository, which a repository administrator maintains, and the registry policy is not enforced there. To govern those servers, control who administers the repository and review the MCP configuration and the agent profiles.
questions.takeaway: Registry only covers the IDEs and Copilot CLI. The cloud agent's MCP servers come from the repository's MCP configuration.

evidence.quote: GitHub supports MCP allowlist enforcement at the organization and enterprise level, tied to the Copilot seat that governs the user.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 3

evidence.quote: Once a policy is selected, it is applied immediately to all developers.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 3

evidence.note: The reference lists the surfaces on which MCP private registry features are supported. Registry display and allowlist enforcement are supported in Copilot CLI and in the IDEs (VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains, Eclipse, Xcode). Both are marked as not supported for Copilot cloud agent. Enforcement applies to both remote and local MCP servers.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

evidence.note: As a repository administrator, you can configure MCP servers for use within your repository.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

questions.title: Case study: Northwind Traders
questions.scenario:
### Overview

Northwind Traders is a wholesale company that develops a warehouse management platform. Northwind Traders has a GitHub organization named Northwind.

### Existing environment

Northwind has a private repository named `warehouse-api` that contains an ASP.NET Core service. The repository has the following configuration:

- The default branch is `main`. A ruleset named RS1 targets `main`. RS1 requires a pull request, one approving review, and a status check named `build-test`.
- A workflow named `ci.yml` runs for pull requests. It reports the `build-test` check and runs a CodeQL analysis. Code scanning alerts are shown in pull requests, but they do not block merging.
- GitHub Copilot cloud agent is enabled for `warehouse-api`. The agent opens pull requests. It cannot merge or deploy.
- An environment named `production` has required reviewers.

A workflow named `release.yml` deploys the service to production. The workflow contains the following lines.

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: main
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh
```

### Planned changes

Northwind plans to implement the following changes:

- Assign two types of issues to the cloud agent: corrections to user interface texts in resource files, and changes to the authentication module.
- Add three custom agents named `planner`, `implementer`, and `test-writer`. The planner will rate the risk of each plan. A workflow will apply low-risk plans automatically and will route all other plans to an approval.
- Add a GitHub Agentic Workflow named `daily-status.md` that summarizes the open issues and creates an issue that contains a status report every day.
- Preinstall the .NET SDK and restore the NuGet packages in the environment of the cloud agent before the agent starts working.

### Problem statements

Northwind identifies the following issues:

- Last month, a faulty release was deployed. The team could not determine which commit was running in production, and the rollback took three hours.
- Three pull requests from the agent were merged although CodeQL had reported new alerts of high severity for them.
- In a Copilot Chat session in Visual Studio Code, a developer and the agent agreed that the retry logic of a task must use the company's shared resilience library. The cloud agent later continued the same task from the pull request and implemented its own retry loop.
- Pull request #482 from the agent has been open for five days. The pull request contains commits. It has no workflow run, no evidence, and no review request.
- Reviewers cannot tell which agent produced a pull request or where the evidence for the pull request is.

### Technical requirements

Northwind identifies the following technical requirements:

- Corrections to user interface texts are low risk and easily reversible. For these issues, speed of iteration is more important than agreeing on a plan in advance. The merge requirements of RS1 must continue to apply.
- The routing of plans by risk must not depend on a person who reads the plan.
- Each production deployment must be traceable to one commit, and a rollback must deploy a known earlier version.
- A pull request must not be merged when code scanning reports a new alert of high or critical severity.
- Decisions about a task must be available to every tool and every session that works on the task.
- In `daily-status.md`, the coding agent must run with read-only permissions. Write operations must be applied by a separate, gated step.
- Every pull request from a custom agent must identify the agent, and the evidence for the pull request must be durable and linked from the pull request.
- All solutions must follow the principle of least privilege and must not weaken the existing controls.

questions.stem:
You need to recommend a workflow for the issues that correct user interface texts.

Which workflow should you recommend?

options.text: A plan-first pull request, in which the plan is approved before any code is written
options.rationale: Incorrect. Plan-first is for changes that are high risk or difficult to reverse. Here it would slow down work for which speed matters more.

options.text: Plan and execution in the same pull request, with the checks and the review of RS1
options.rationale: Correct. The changes are low risk and easily reversible, and iteration speed matters. The plan stays visible, and RS1 still gates the merge.

options.text: Direct commits by the agent to `main`, with the plan in each commit message
options.rationale: Incorrect. That bypasses the pull request, the review and the check that RS1 requires.

options.text: Plan and execution in the same pull request, with the agent on the bypass list of RS1
options.rationale: Incorrect. A bypass actor can merge without meeting RS1, which weakens the existing controls.

questions.explanation: Both workflows are reviewed before the merge. They differ in when code may be generated. For low-risk, easily reversible changes for which speed and iteration matter, the plan and the code can be in the same pull request, with the required checks and the reviews kept. Plan-first is reserved for high-risk work such as the authentication module.
questions.takeaway: Low risk and reversible → plan and execution in one pull request, checks and reviews unchanged.

evidence.quote: speed and iteration are more important
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 4

evidence.quote: changes are low-risk or easily reversible
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 4

evidence.quote: Use plan + execution for medium/low risk work, but keep checks/reviews required.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 4

whyExam.skill: Configure agent planning to be distinct from agent execution

clues.text: M2 unit 4 has a list "When to use each option" and explicit decision guidance.
Plan-first sounds safer, so it is tempting to choose it everywhere.

questions.stem:
You need to recommend how the `planner` agent reports the risk of a plan to meet the technical requirements.

What should you recommend?

options.text: A paragraph in the pull request description that explains the risk
options.rationale: Incorrect. A narrative must be read and interpreted by a person before the plan can be routed.

options.text: A label that a reviewer adds to the pull request after reading the plan
options.rationale: Incorrect. The routing would depend on the reviewer, which the requirement excludes.

options.text: A sentence at the end of the session log that states the risk level
options.rationale: Incorrect. A workflow cannot route reliably on free text in a log.

options.text: A `risk` field in a machine-readable plan file that is uploaded as an artifact
options.rationale: Correct. A workflow can read the field and route the plan, for example to automatic application or to an approval.

questions.explanation: A plan that drives automation must be structured. When the planner writes the risk rating as a field of a machine-readable file such as `plan.json`, a job can read it, expose it as an output, and route the plan. A rating that exists only as prose depends on interpretation, and the routing is then not enforced consistently.
questions.takeaway: A structured plan carries its risk as a machine-readable field, and the workflow routes on it.

evidence.quote: Decision guidance: Don't rely on narrative explanations of risk. Use a machine-readable signal and enforce routing.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.quote: When an agent produces a plan with a risk rating, that rating should determine how the system responds.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.quote: plan.json (machine-readable)
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 6

whyExam.skill: Configure an agent to output a structured plan

clues.text: The bullet names the structured plan.
M6 unit 2 decision guidance: use a machine-readable signal and enforce routing.
The unit reads `risk` from `plan.json` in workflow YAML.

questions.stem:
You need to change `release.yml` to meet the technical requirements for production deployments.

What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a commit SHA or a tag that is passed to the workflow, and remove `ref: main`.
options.rationale: Correct. Each deployment then refers to one explicit commit, and a rollback deploys the reference of a known earlier version.

options.text: Keep `ref: main`, and add a `concurrency` group named `production` to the job.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A concurrency group keeps deployments from overlapping. The job would still deploy whatever `main` contains when it starts.

options.text: Deploy from a branch named `stable` that is updated after each merge into `main`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is still the latest commit of a branch. Nothing records which commit a given deployment used.

options.text: Keep `ref: main`, and increase the number of required reviewers of `production`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. More reviewers do not make the deployed commit identifiable.

questions.explanation: `ref: main` checks out the latest commit of the branch at the moment the job starts, which can be later than the commit that was approved. The rollback-safe pattern is to operate on explicit references. A commit SHA or a tag identifies exactly what is deployed, and rolling back means deploying the previous reference.
questions.takeaway: Deploy explicit references, a commit SHA or a tag, never "latest on a branch".

evidence.quote: Operate on explicit references (commit/tag) when deploying sensitive configuration, rather than "latest on a branch."
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.quote: Rollback readiness: high-risk changes include rollback notes and scope limits.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

whyExam.skill: Implement rollbacks

clues.text: "Implement rollbacks" is a named bullet.
M2 unit 7 calls this the rollback-safe pattern.

questions.stem:
You need to create the workflow file that prepares the environment of GitHub Copilot cloud agent to meet the planned changes.

How should you complete the workflow?
questions.template:
# File: .github/workflows/[[file]]
name: "Copilot Setup Steps"

on:
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  [[job]]:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: [[perm]]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with:
          dotnet-version: '9.0.x'
      - run: dotnet restore

file.rationale: The agent's environment is customized with a workflow file at the fixed path `.github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml`.

job.rationale: The file must contain a single job that is named `copilot-setup-steps`. A job with another name is not picked up.

perm.rationale: The steps clone the repository to restore the packages, which needs `contents: read`. Write access is not needed, and the agent gets its own token for its work.

questions.explanation: The cloud agent works in an ephemeral environment that is powered by GitHub Actions. The steps of the `copilot-setup-steps` job run before the agent starts, so the SDK and the packages are in place. The file name and the job name are fixed, the permissions are set as low as the steps allow, and the file must be on the default branch.
questions.takeaway: `.github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml`, one job named `copilot-setup-steps`, lowest permissions, default branch.

evidence.quote: On GitHub, Copilot in the cloud works in a GitHub Actions-powered environment, creates changes on a branch, and prepares those changes for review.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 5

evidence.note: You customize Copilot's environment with a workflow file located at `.github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml`. The file must contain a single `copilot-setup-steps` job, and its steps are executed before Copilot starts working. The example sets the permissions to the lowest that the steps need: `contents: read` if the steps clone the repository. The workflow won't trigger unless it is present on the default branch.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Configure an agent to handle environment-specific constraints

clues.text: The audience profile of the study guide names "Copilot setup steps".
The file path and the job name are fixed, which makes an exact drop-down item.

questions.stem:
You need to complete the frontmatter of `daily-status.md` to meet the technical requirements.

A write action, such as creating an issue, is declared as a safe output: the agent proposes it, and a separate gated step decides what is allowed and applies it.

questions.stem:
You need to prevent a repetition of the issue with the retry logic and meet the related technical requirement.

What should you do?

options.text: Repeat the decision in the prompt of every tool that works on the task.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Copies in prompts are session context. They can diverge, and a tool that does not get the prompt does not know the decision.

options.text: Ask the developer to keep the same Copilot Chat session open until the task is merged.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The context of a chat session in the IDE is not available to the cloud agent.

options.text: Store the decision as a user-level preference in Copilot Memory.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A user-level preference belongs to one person, and a stored memory is not a guaranteed input for every session on the task.

options.text: Record the decision in the description of the pull request.
options.rationale: Correct. The pull request is the place for decisions and progress, and every tool that works on the task can read it.

questions.explanation: State is shared through durable references, not through session context. The decision existed only in a chat session, so the cloud agent could not know it. Decisions and progress live in the pull request. Any tool or session that continues the task re-anchors to it and finds the decision there.
questions.takeaway: A decision that matters goes into the pull request, never only into a chat.

evidence.quote: Decisions and progress live in pull requests
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

evidence.quote: Avoid storing critical information only in prompts or chat history
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

evidence.quote: Always write important updates to issues or pull requests
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

whyExam.skill: Share agent state

clues.text: "Share agent state" is a named bullet.
M5 unit 4: avoid storing critical information only in prompts or chat history.

questions.stem:
You need to meet the technical requirement for code scanning alerts.

You need to classify the state of pull request #482.

Which failure mode should you identify?

options.text: Flapping
options.rationale: Incorrect. Flapping means that workflows rerun repeatedly without converging. This pull request has no workflow run at all.

options.text: Conflicting outputs
options.rationale: Incorrect. Conflicting outputs are pull requests that compete and block each other. Only one pull request is involved.

options.text: A stalled workflow
options.rationale: Incorrect. A stalled workflow has checks that fail repeatedly or an approval that never arrives. Here no check ran and no review was requested.

options.text: Partial execution
options.rationale: Correct. The pull request exists, but the evidence and the validation are missing.

questions.stem:
You need to meet the technical requirement for the pull requests of the three custom agents.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Use a title prefix and a label that name the agent, such as `[agent: implementer]`.
options.rationale: Correct. Consistent attribution in titles and labels shows which agent produced a pull request.

options.text: Let the three agents push to one shared branch, so that their work is in one pull request.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A shared branch interleaves commits and makes it harder to attribute a change to an agent.

options.text: Upload each agent's report as a workflow artifact, and link the run in an Evidence section.
options.rationale: Correct. The artifact is durable evidence, and the link makes it reachable from the pull request.

options.text: Ask each agent to describe its results in the last comment of its session log.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A description is the agent's own account, and it is not linked from the pull request.

options.text: Apply one label named `automation` to every pull request that an agent opens.
options.rationale: Incorrect. One label for all agents does not identify which agent produced a pull request.

questions.explanation: As the number of agents grows, reviewers need to know which agent produced a change and what evidence supports it. Attribution comes from conventions: a title prefix, a label, and standard sections in the body. Evidence comes from artifacts that are uploaded by the workflow and linked from the pull request.
questions.takeaway: Attribution: title prefix and label for each agent. Evidence: uploaded artifacts, linked from the pull request.

questions.stem:
Northwind plans to increase the autonomy of the agents step by step.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

items.statement: With propose-only autonomy, an agent can create branches and pull requests, and it cannot merge or deploy.
items.explanation: That is the definition of the propose-only level, and it is the level that the cloud agent has in `warehouse-api` today.

items.statement: The number of changed lines is sufficient to determine the risk level of a change.
items.explanation: Risk also depends on where the change is applied, how easily it can be reversed, and how quickly it affects users or systems.

items.statement: Full automation is appropriate for a change that cannot be reversed, provided that the required checks pass.
items.explanation: Full automation is used only when failures are reversible. Irreversible actions require approval.

questions.explanation: Autonomy is granted in levels and matched to risk. Propose-only lets an agent create branches and pull requests. Wider levels are added as the agent proves reliable, and each level is bounded by the impact and the reversibility of the actions, not by the size of a change or by a green check.
questions.takeaway: Autonomy follows impact and reversibility. Full automation only for reversible failures.
